phase1.intro:
Now that you know a class can implement several interfaces at once, here's the one wrinkle that comes with it.

Want to see the conflict first, or the flexibility it buys you?

topics.buttonText: What happens when two interfaces both define the same default method?
dialogue: Look at FlyingCar: both `Drivable` and `Flyable` provide their own default `honk()`. [[warn:What happens when two interfaces both define a DEFAULT method with the exact same name]]?

[[key:Java refuses to just silently pick one for you]] — that would be guessing. Instead, FlyingCar is required to override `honk()` itself, using `Drivable.super.honk()` to say "specifically call Drivable's version," or writing entirely new logic.

stickyNote.flavor: ⚔️ Java won't guess, you must resolve it
stickyNote.definition: When two implemented interfaces share a default method name, the class must override it explicitly — e.g. Drivable.super.honk() to pick one.

topics.buttonText: What's the real benefit of implementing several interfaces?
dialogue: `AmphibiousVehicle implements Drivable, Swimmable` can be treated as EITHER type depending on what a piece of code needs — `Drivable asDrivable = amphib;` only exposes drive-related behavior, `Swimmable asSwimmable = amphib;` only exposes swim-related behavior.
Same object, different lenses depending on which interface reference you're looking through it with.

stickyNote.flavor: 🔍 same object, different lens per interface
stickyNote.definition: One object implementing several interfaces can be referenced through any of them, exposing only that interface's methods through that reference.

topics.buttonText: Why doesn't Java have the diamond problem?
dialogue: This is exactly why Java avoids the notorious [[term:diamond problem]] that multiple CLASS inheritance runs into: interfaces don't carry state, only behavior contracts, so [[key:the only real ambiguity that can ever arise is conflicting default methods]] — and Java forces you to resolve that explicitly.

stickyNote.flavor: 💎 avoided because interfaces carry no state
stickyNote.definition: The diamond problem plagues multiple class inheritance with ambiguous state. Java's interfaces carry no state, so the only ambiguity is conflicting default methods, which must be resolved explicitly.

phase1.openingDialogue: Implementing multiple interfaces is flexible — until two default methods share a name, and Java makes you resolve it yourself. ⚔️

phase2.errorMessage:
C.java:17: error: class C inherits unrelated defaults for hello() from types A and B
class C implements A, B {
^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:Both A and B define their own default hello(), and C implements both]] — Java has two equally valid candidates and zero way to know which one you actually meant, so it refuses to compile rather than silently guess wrong.

[[key:The fix is to override hello() in C yourself and pick explicitly]]: `A.super.hello()` to use A's version, `B.super.hello()` for B's, or write brand new logic entirely. [[key:This exact rule — force an explicit resolution instead of silently picking one — is precisely why Java's multiple interface implementation avoids the classic diamond problem]] that plagues true multiple inheritance.

phase3.openingDialogue: Why settle for one when you can have many? Multiple interfaces! 🎯

mcq.question:
What must a class do if it implements two interfaces that both provide a default method with the same signature?

A) Nothing — Java automatically picks the first interface listed
B) Override that method itself and explicitly resolve which version (or write new logic)
C) It's a compile error with no possible fix
D) Remove one of the interfaces

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create interfaces:
1. Eatable — void eat()
2. Sleepable — void sleep()
3. Playable — void play()

Create a class Pet that implements all three.
In main, create a Pet and call all three methods.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: the "diamond problem" gets its name from the literal shape you'd draw if you diagrammed it — one base class at the top, two classes branching from it, then one class inheriting from both of those, forming a diamond. It's one of the most-cited reasons C++ allows multiple class inheritance but Java deliberately doesn't.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you mix more capabilities~
